scenarios.title: Remain useful higher than the board battle
scenarios.objective: Recognize high support while teammates contest the puck low.
scenarios.briefing: F1 and Gold 1 contest a loose puck along the attacking-zone side boards. F2 is closer to Gold’s net than they are. YOU are the high forward; this exercise assigns YOU to support higher than the battle until control changes. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.
cues: The puck marker is separate from F1 and Gold 1, as the briefing states.

questions.prompt: What is the puck state at the board battle?
questions.explanation: The puck marker is separate from F1 and Gold 1, as the briefing states.

questions.prompt: Which two jobs could high support serve?

options.text: Guaranteed possession merely by standing high
Help against a counterattack if Gold wins
An outlet if Navy wins control

questions.explanation: High support can preserve options in either outcome, but does not win the battle itself.

questions.prompt: Arrange a read from high support behind the battle.

options.text: Check the high-slot space and opposing outlet

questions.explanation: The high role is this exercise’s stated plan; a coach may assign a different forecheck elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a useful high-slot support example without joining the scrum.
questions.explanation: The reference keeps separation from the wall contest and access to middle ice. Other distances may suit the play.

questions.prompt: If F1 wins clean possession and looks inside, what could you offer?

options.text: An automatic move into F1’s crowded wall space
A claim that the puck remains loose

questions.explanation: Control permits an attacking read, but you still need a reachable lane.

questions.prompt: Explain why the high forward’s position matters before the battle is decided.
questions.explanation: Describe both the possible outlet and defensive recovery roles, using the opponent’s location.

questions.prompt: Which Navy player is assigned the high support role?
questions.explanation: YOU is the assigned high Navy forward supporting above the loose-puck battle; if F1 wins, offer the high outlet, while a Gold win changes YOU to recovery.

questions.prompt: Which two jobs can high support serve?

options.text: Be a reset if F1 wins it
Recover inside if Gold wins it

questions.explanation: High separation supports either possession outcome; joining the battle removes balance.

questions.prompt: Move YOU slightly higher and inside, above the board battle.
questions.explanation: The high-inside position keeps both puck outcomes visible and protects the middle; if F1 wins cleanly, lower into the next support lane.

questions.prompt: Why should high support remain useful before the battle is decided?
questions.explanation: Ownership is unknown, so a balanced position can attack or recover without guessing; once control is clear, move to the new job.

scenarios.title: Look across from the half wall

The coach asks you to look for a clearly visible passing connection, without assuming a cross-ice pass is safe. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.
cues: The forwards are on opposite sides of the high slot.

questions.prompt: Which named area lies between the two forward positions?

options.text: The defending crease at the Navy net

questions.explanation: The forwards are on opposite sides of the high slot.

questions.prompt: Select two checks for an inside passing connection.

options.text: Whether F1 can see your target
Whether Gold 2 can reach the lane
Whether every cross-ice pass is automatically available

questions.explanation: Both the route and the carrier’s view matter; a large empty-looking space is not proof of safety.

questions.prompt: Arrange one way to create a clearer lane.

options.text: Identify the defender crossing the route
Change your angle through useful space

questions.explanation: The movement may create a pass or move a defender for another teammate.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward a high-slot pocket that changes the passing angle.
questions.explanation: This offers a shorter inside connection than the original far-side position. Gold 2’s response still needs checking.

questions.prompt: Gold 2 shifts into the high-slot connection. What might help now?

options.text: Use another support angle or leave room for D1
Assume the old connection remains clear
Treat Gold 2 as irrelevant because the pass is cross-ice

questions.explanation: The new defender position changes the read; the first support target is not permanent.

questions.prompt: Name the space you moved into and explain what made its passing angle different.
questions.explanation: Use “high slot” if describing the central pocket; connect the name to F1, Gold 2 and the route rather than only naming a zone.

questions.prompt: What should YOU call if Gold 2 enters the high-slot connection?

options.text: The lane is clear because Gold 2 moved

questions.explanation: Calling the inside lane tells F1 that Gold 2 has entered the connection and helps coordinate the next look; if the lane is still blocked, keep the puck moving only when another route is visible.

questions.prompt: Which two cues decide whether a cross-ice look is usable?

options.text: Assuming distance makes the pass safe

questions.explanation: Defender positions and a visible receiver determine the lane; distance alone does not make a pass safe.

questions.prompt: Move YOU into a high-slot pocket that changes F1’s passing angle.
questions.explanation: The pocket gives F1 a clearer angle while keeping separation from Gold 1 and Gold 2; if a defender fills it, re-space.

questions.prompt: Name the space you moved into and explain what made its angle different.
questions.explanation: The high-slot pocket changes the line between F1 and YOU and may move the defender’s stick lane; if Gold 2 shifts across, inspect the new obstruction.

scenarios.title: Settle a difficult pass before choosing
scenarios.objective: Notice when control needs to be established before the next action.
scenarios.briefing: A pass has bounced just ahead of YOU in the neutral zone. F2 is higher up ice. Gold 1 is approaching but not yet on the puck. The exercise states that YOU have not settled it. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.
cues: The briefing explicitly says the pass is unsettled, matching the loose marker.

questions.prompt: Has YOU established possession in this freeze?

options.text: No, the pass is still loose
Yes, the puck is secured on the stick

questions.explanation: The briefing explicitly says the pass is unsettled, matching the loose marker.

questions.prompt: Which two cues affect the next action?

options.text: The quality of the arriving pass
A rule that every pass must be one-touched
How soon Gold 1 can pressure it

questions.explanation: Control and pressure determine what is practical; one-touch passing is not always available.

questions.prompt: Arrange one response to a difficult neutral-zone pass.

options.text: Read the bounce and approaching pressure
Establish control if there is time

questions.explanation: Emergency touches may be needed under tighter pressure; this sequence assumes time to settle.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to an example position for collecting the unsettled puck.
questions.explanation: The position moves toward the puck without pretending it is already controlled. Stick reach and bounce remain unmodelled.

questions.prompt: If the puck arrives flat and F2’s lane is clearly available, what might change?

options.text: You must always take several extra touches
Gold 1 no longer needs to be checked
An earlier pass may be practical

questions.explanation: A better reception can create an earlier option, but only while the lane remains available.

questions.prompt: What would you need to see before recommending a one-touch pass here?
questions.explanation: Mention the puck’s arrival quality, receiver readiness and pressure on the route.

questions.prompt: What should YOU call while F2’s lane is available but the puck is unsettled?

options.text: Not settled; give me a short option
One-touch now no matter the pressure

questions.explanation: The call tells F2 that support exists while YOU still needs control, so the pass can wait for a readable touch; if pressure closes the short option, secure the puck first.

questions.prompt: Which two cues affect the next touch?

options.text: The pass being difficult no longer matters

questions.explanation: F2’s lane and Gold 1’s pressure shape whether to settle, protect or move it; a difficult reception remains relevant.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to an example collecting position behind the bounced puck and away from Gold 1.
questions.explanation: The offset position gives YOU room to settle while seeing F2 and Gold 1; if the puck jumps away, recover rather than forcing a pass.

questions.prompt: What would you need to see before recommending a one-touch pass?
questions.explanation: Look for settled control, a visible lane to F2, and enough time that Gold 1 cannot immediately close the touch; if any cue is missing, secure the puck first. A one-touch is an option, not a promise.

Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.
cues: The puck is loose between opponents and no winner is stated.
